title: Exploration into formal aesthetics in design: (material) texture

findings.consequent: 'texture' defined as 'the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of surface or bulk of materials/objects'
findings.quote: We propose to define 'texture' as 'the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of surface or bulk of materials/objects'.

findings.consequent: 'perceived texture' defined as 'a synthesis of physiological and psychological response and impression to the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of the surface or the bulk of materials/objects'
findings.quote: Correspondingly, we propose a definition of perceived texture as 'a synthesis of physiological and psychological response and impression to the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of the surface or the bulk of materials/objects'.

findings.antecedent: Understanding the correlation between objective texture attributes (physical parameters) and subjective texture perception
findings.consequent: Framework for creating suitable, aesthetic material textures
findings.quote: The understanding of the correlation between the objective texture attributes (usually represented by physical parameters) and the subjective texture perception will provide the framework for creating suitable, aesthetic material textures.

findings.consequent: Can be summarized into four dimensions: geometrical, physical-chemical, emotional, and associative
findings.quote: the subjective description of material texture can be summarised into four dimensions: geometrical dimension, physical-chemical dimension, emotional dimension and associative dimension.

findings.consequent: Includes macro impression (surface pattern, e.g., plain-bumpy, regular-irregular) and micro feeling (surface roughness, e.g., smooth-rough, fine-coarse)
findings.quote: The texture lexicons within geometrical dimension include the description of a material surface in two aspects: One is the global, macro impression of the surface configuration... The other is the local, micro feeling of the surface configuration...

findings.consequent: Describes subjective response to physical/chemical attributes (e.g., warm-cold, hard-soft, moist-dry, shiny-non-shiny, sticky-non-sticky)
findings.quote: This dimension describes the subjective response to the physical and/or chemical attributes of a material surface. It includes the dynamic characters that need energy exchange... High-frequency lexicons used in this dimension include such as: warm – cold, hard – soft, moist – dry, shiny – non-shiny, sticky – non-sticky, etc.

findings.consequent: Describes affective, hedonic, valuable feelings evoked by touching material surface (e.g., comfortable-uncomfortable, lively/cheerful-dull, elegant-ugly, modern-traditional)
findings.quote: This dimension describes the affective, hedonic, valuable feelings that are evoked by touching the material surface. High-frequency lexicons in this dimension include such as: comfortable – uncomfortable, lively/cheerful – dull, elegant – ugly, modern – traditional, etc.

findings.consequent: Describes subjective association from the material to existing things in perceiver's life experience
findings.quote: This dimension describes the subjective association from the material, i.e. to what existing things in the perceiver's life experience can the texture be compared.

findings.antecedent: Certain physical parameters of materials (e.g., roughness, hardness)
findings.consequent: Underlie or correspond to subjective descriptions of texture
findings.quote: There are often certain physical parameters of materials that underlie or correspond to subjective descriptions of texture.

findings.consequent: Physical parameters such as roughness and hardness
findings.quote: We have conducted experimental research to find a relationship between subjective feeling of materials with physical parameters such as roughness and hardness [14].
The relationship between physical roughness and psychological roughness tends to conform to a power law [7] [14].

findings.antecedent: Texture generation (for material or image textures)
findings.consequent: Can be derived from nature, mind & fantasy, innovation in science & technology, virtual reality, micro-world, and social events
findings.quote: Texture can be generated or learnt from nature, mind & fantasy, innovation in science & technology, virtual reality, micro-world and social events.

limitations: Texture is a less identified property compared to color, and little is understood about how humans respond to and perceive it (Abstract, Page 2).
Texture is ambiguous and difficult to identify compared to properties like color or sound (Section 1, Page 2).
Character dimensions for texture description vary between researchers, lacking systematic classification (Section 4, Page 6).
The discrimination between surface pattern (macro) and surface roughness (micro) is sometimes ambiguous (Section 4, Page 6).
Associative lexicons for texture are random and low frequency, despite being rich in description (Section 4, Page 7).
minimum_safe_summary: The paper explores formal aesthetics in design, focusing on material texture. It defines texture as the geometrical and physical-chemical attributes of surfaces and perceived texture as the synthesis of physiological and psychological responses to these attributes. The authors propose that subjective texture descriptions can be categorized into geometrical, physical-chemical, emotional, and associative dimensions. They highlight the need to understand the psychophysical relationship between objective material parameters (like roughness and hardness) and subjective perceptions, noting that this relationship often follows a power law. The paper also identifies various sources for texture generation, including nature, human imagination, virtual reality, scientific and technological advancements, the micro-world, and social events, emphasizing the multisensory and culturally influenced nature of texture perception in design. A key limitation is the current lack of systematic understanding and classification of texture compared to other sensory properties.
